10125-the-best-letters-of-charles-lamb:
This selection of Charles Lamb's best letters carries praise from Swinburne, who thought the Essays of Elia would keep their perfume and Lamb's letters their sweet savor when grander books lay dusty. Hazlitt's judgment adds that no assemblage of letters of such range, period, and typical character had ever been produced.

The letters run largely to Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Lamb's great friend, with wit, gossip, and feeling on every page. Readers meet Elia himself, not the essayist alone: funny, loyal, and tender. It is the best way to know one of England's most loved writers.
14456-the-uphill-climb:
B. M. Bower's 1913 western novel follows Ford, a restless ranchman who wakes married to a woman whose name he does not know. Illustrations by Charles M. Russell accompany the Grosset and Dunlap edition.

Ford flees the entanglement and works as foreman of the Double Cross. He wrestles with drink, pride, and the memory of an Alaska deal, while friends such as Mason and Kate press him toward honesty. Bower's dialogue is brisk and funny, and the Montana ranch setting feels lived in. The novel is a lively tale of a man climbing out of his own mess.
17977-charles-lamb:
Walter Jerrold wrote this short life of Charles Lamb for Bell's Miniature Series of Great Writers, printed in London in 1905. Lamb, the gentle essayist of London, is best known as Elia, whose essays on roast pig, old books, and city life won him lasting fame.

Jerrold traces Lamb's life, his poems, plays, stories, verses, and letters, then turns to the Essays of Elia and Lamb's plain, quaint style. A list of works and a note on later lives close the book. It is a compact, kind introduction, made for readers who want to meet Lamb before they read Elia himself.
24592-the-tale-of-snowball-lamb:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this children's animal tale, part of his Slumber-Town Tales series, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. The series follows the Muley Cow, Old Dog Spot, Grunty Pig, Henrietta Hen, Turkey Proudfoot, Pony Twinkleheels, and Miss Kitty Cat. Its heroine here is Snowball Lamb.

A frontispiece picture shows Henrietta Hen warning Snowball to get out of the way. Bailey's tale follows the lamb through farmyard adventures, with gentle humour and short chapters for bedtime. Small children get a soft, woolly story of farm animals, told in the simple style of Bailey's best-loved books.
2519-a-popular-account-of-dr-livingstone:
David Livingstone wrote this account of the Zambesi expedition of 1858 to 1864, drawing on notes kept by his brother Charles, who served under him. The party traveled up the Zambesi river, mapped its tributaries, and reached Lakes Shirwa and Nyassa in the heart of southeast Africa.

Livingstone describes the land, its peoples, its chiefs, and its trade, and he argues plainly against the slave trade that ravaged the region. The book mixes travel, natural history, and missionary purpose, and it shaped how Victorian readers pictured inner Africa. It remains a key firsthand record of a journey that opened new maps and new debates.
26619-minnie-s-pet-lamb:
Nannie, a South Down lamb with bright black eyes and a brownish-gray face, is the heroine of this 1864 children's book by Mrs. Madeline Leslie. Brought home crying by Mr. Lee, Nannie is penned beside Star the Shetland pony's stall, climbs the railing, and gives her whole heart to the pony. Star returns the love, neighing softly and taking care never to step on her.

Pasture days, barn-yard separations, and breakfast calls follow, with Nannie following Star wherever he goes. Later anecdotes widen to other sheep, including a shepherd with six hundred pure Merinos who rules his flock by horn and salt. The book teaches kindness to animals through one lamb's friendship, in Leslie's Minnie and Her Pets series.
26856-solander-s-radio-tomb:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote this comic story about the early days of radio, when fans argued endlessly over crystal sets against tube sets. Its narrator opens mid-quarrel on the 8:15 train to New York. He tells his friend Murchison that only a half-baked lunatic would prefer crystal's clear, sharp reception to a tube set's distant stations. Remington Solander, sitting behind them with his long sheeplike face, leans forward and asks to talk radio.

Solander is the richest man in town, worth three million dollars at his death, and he has spent his life copying religious quotations, hymns, and sermons into fourteen volumes by hand. He enlists the narrator, a trustee of the cemetery association, for his burial scheme, and the title gives it away: Solander means to carry radio into his tomb. Butler wrings the comedy from a plan that changes as fast as radio itself.
2797-the-wolves-and-the-lamb:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote this play of wolves and a lamb, with Horace Milliken, a wealthy widowed city merchant, and his child George at its center. Captain Touchit, Clarence Kicklebury, and the butler John Howell crowd a household of schemers.

Lady Kicklebury's servant Bulkeley and a footboy named Charles Page add to the comedy of manners, as fortune hunters circle a widower and his son. Thackeray writes with stage wit about money, marriage, and family. The play offers his satire in dialogue, sharp and humane. The stage gives Thackeray's satire a sharper edge.
28886-the-hickory-limb:
Parker Fillmore wrote this 1907 children's book, illustrated by Rose Cecil O'Neill and published by Harcourt, Brace. The title comes from the nursery rhyme about a mother who lets her daughter go swimming, telling her to hang her clothes on a hickory limb and not go near the water. The story follows Gladys Bailey, who plans to teach the twins Katherine and Alice the mystery of formal calls.

Gladys, carrying a parasol and a card case, decides four are too many for calling and slips away without little Margery. Margery chases them, crying wait, and the twins barely slip through the gate. Fillmore writes with humor about children's social pretensions, and O'Neill's pictures catch the pond, the dare, and the tight places. Readers get a light, funny period children's book.
6064-memoirs-of-lady-fanshawe-wife-of-si:
Anne, Lady Fanshawe, wife of Sir Richard Fanshawe, ambassador from Charles II to Portugal and Madrid, wrote her own memoirs, here edited by Beatrice Marshall with extracts from her husband's correspondence. The introduction finds a deathless charm in the middle of the seventeenth century, a period of upheaval and turmoil.

A stately, debonair court was swept away by civil war flames, an usurper reigned, and a fallen dynasty returned. The trial and execution of Charles Stuart still appeal to imagination and touch hearts that bring sentiment to history. Fanshawe's pages give that age through a wife's eyes, close to courts and exile.
a-popular-account-of-dr-livingstone-s-ex:
David Livingstone gives a popular account of his expedition to the Zambesi and its tributaries from 1858 to 1864, as the title page of the 1894 John Murray edition states. He dedicates the book to Lord Palmerston, praising his policy against the slave trade on Africa's west coast and urging the same care for the east. His brother Charles served under him on the expedition.

The narrative follows the river past rapids and fever country, the discovery of Lakes Shirwa and Nyassa, and dealings with the peoples along the banks. Livingstone reports honestly on the expedition's failures, including the death of his wife, Mary. The book is both exploration record and argument for opening Africa to lawful trade.
addison-analysis-of-the-report-of-the-co:
Analysis of the Report of the Committee of the Virginia Assembly, published in 1800 by Alexander Addison, is an American political pamphlet of the early republic. Its subject is a report of a committee of the Virginia Assembly, written on the proceedings of several other states. Those states had sent answers to Virginia's resolutions, and the committee's report judged their replies.

Addison takes that report apart point by point, in the heated argument over states' answers to Virginia that followed the resolutions of the late 1790s. The pamphlet is a piece of the first great American debate about federal power and state protest. It preserves the reasoning of a Federalist-era judge writing for the public in a pamphlet war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-tomb:
An altar tomb is an oblong tomb or monument over a grave, covered with a slab or table resembling an altar. Its oblong form follows the grave beneath, the slab closing the monument like an altar table. The table may stand bare or carry one or more recumbent sculptured figures. It may stand free with all four sides exposed, or with one side against the wall.

Where one side meets the wall, a canopy or niche often rises above it. Free-standing examples show the monument from every side, while wall examples gain their canopy as a frame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-ferdina:
Baron Ferdinand de Géramb, in religion Brother Mary Joseph, was Abbot and procurator-general of La Trappe. Born at Lyons in 1772 of a noble Hungarian family, he died at Rome in 1848. A fiery, chivalrous soldier against the French Revolution, he rose to lieutenant-general. Napoleon imprisoned him at Vincennes in 1808, holding him until the allies entered Paris in 1814.

Bidding farewell to Tsar and Austrian Emperor, he left the world and took Trappist vows in 1817. In 1830 he faced down insurgents bent on pillaging Mt Olivet, sparing the abbey its horrors. After a Jerusalem pilgrimage, he became procurator-general at Rome in 1833, winning Gregory XVI's esteem. Though no priest, he was named titular abbot with ring and pectoral cross, and his travel writings won wide translation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-education-of-:
Teaching deaf children is the subject of this long entry, which starts by clearing up its own title. People born deaf, or deaf from early childhood, do not speak because they cannot hear speech to copy. The entry says their voice organs may still be sound. It prefers the term deaf-mute, and later simply deaf, since the old phrase deaf and dumb wrongly hints at a fault in both hearing and voice.

From early manual alphabets the survey moves to the great method debate. One side taught by signs and writing. The other side, the oral method pressed by Heinicke in Germany, trained pupils to speak and lip-read. It traces schools, teachers, and meetings where sign language serves large crowds. It closes on the spiritual care of deaf Catholics. Few priests in the United States then gave time to that work, it notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Nothomb, a Belgian statesman born at Messancy in 1805 and dead at Berlin in 1881, helped write Belgium into being. Schooled at Luxemburg and trained in law at Liège, he took his doctorate in 1826 and practised in Luxemburg and Brussels, pressing the Belgian cause in the press.

During the 1830 rising Nothomb hurried back to Brussels, served as secretary to the committee drafting the first constitution, and sat as the assembly's youngest member. He fought both union with France and a republic, backing a representative monarchy with two houses, a free press, and church and state each free in its own sphere. From 1831 to 1836 he ran foreign affairs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-lamb:
The paschal lamb was the lamb Israelites were commanded to eat with special rites at Passover. Exodus 12 first records the ordinance. To escape the death of Egypt's firstborn, each family was to take an unblemished male lamb of one year on the tenth day of the first month. They kept it to the fourteenth, and sacrificed it in the evening. Its blood, sprinkled on transom and doorposts, marked houses for protection.

The lamb was roasted whole, head, feet, and entrails. It was eaten with unleavened bread and wild lettuce, in haste, loins girded, shoes on, staves in hand, for it is the Lord's Passage. Leftovers were burnt by morning. Numbers and Deuteronomy repeat the rule in shorter form, adding sheep and oxen, and the entry closes by reading the lamb as a figure of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomb:
A tomb is a memorial for the dead at the place of burial, customary among nearly all peoples, above all for distinguished persons. It matters greatly to art history, since the growth of sculpture can be traced almost wholly through tombs, which, standing as a rule in churches, survive better than other works. Apart from catacomb slabs, portrait sarcophagi and scattered mausolea, tombs fall into four classes.

First come tombs with recumbent stones set in church floors, the oldest Christian monuments, bearing a long-shafted cross and, from the eleventh century, the figure of the dead. Next come detached altar-tombs, raised above the burial, plain in Romanesque work and crowded with small figures in Gothic. Wall tombs and free-standing monuments follow, and modern burial outside churches has bred a new sepulchral art, at its best in works such as Bartolome's monument at Pere Lachaise.
doe-osti-3383025-complete-the-design-cos: Packed beds got design-costed, and this DOE text completes tubular designs. The pages detail the estimate findings. The engineers get their data. The instructions were operating. The data were engineer. The packed-bed were tubular. The bench-scale were operating.
govdocs-archive_org-ifePhilipTheNazisBig:
Philip Rife wrote The Nazis' Big Apple A-Bomb for the March/April 2013 issue of the Barnes Review. His claim is a large one: that Germany possessed nuclear weapons during the Second World War and planned to bomb New York with them.

Rife assembles testimony, documents, and inference to argue that the German bomb program went far beyond the failed effort described in standard histories. Mainstream historians hold that Germany never came close to a bomb, so the article stands as revisionist military history. It is presented as an archive holding, without endorsement, for readers of that debate.
memoirs-of-lady-fanshawe-wife-of-sir-ric:
Ann Fanshawe wrote the memoirs of her husband, Sir Richard Fanshawe. He served Charles II as envoy to Portugal and Madrid. Beatrice Marshall edited this edition, with a note on its pictures.

The intro praises the mid 1600s as a time of charm and storm. Civil war, a king's trial, and the throne restored fill that span. Fanshawe wrote late in life, for her one son who lived to manhood. Fourteen children were born to her, and most died young abroad. Most of those children rest in foreign churchyards, she notes. Loss at home sits beside state craft in her plain tale.
nasa-tm-19640019314-satellite-situation-:
The Space Operations Control Center at Goddard issued this report on June 30, 1964. It is volume four, number twelve of the satellite situation series. Data came from Goddard, NORAD, and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. The table lists each object in orbit with its orbital facts.

Explorer 1, from February 1958, still heads the launch list. Rocket bodies are cataloged beside the satellites they carried. Columns give period, tilt, high point, low point, and radio frequency. Lunik 1 and Pioneer 4 are marked as circling the Sun instead. The issue is a dated snapshot of all that humans had placed in space by mid-1964.
nasa-tm-19640023261-satellite-situation-: Volume four, number fifteen of NASA's satellite situation report series is preserved here. Reports in the series were compiled by Goddard Space Flight Center with NORAD and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. Catalog notes say this issue lists orbit data and transmitting frequencies for satellites then in orbit. The hosted sample preserves only garbled table data with no readable text, so this issue's date and listings cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660024016-wind-tunnel-investig:
John E Grimaud at Langley tested three lifting reentry shapes in a wind tunnel at Mach 2.91, for this March 1961 memorandum. Angles of attack ran up to ninety degrees. A lifting reentry body glides as it returns, rather than falling like a capsule. It must stay stable across a huge range of attitudes, some of them far from normal flight.

Grimaud measured stability and control for all three shapes. High-angle data are the hard part of such a test program. A shape that misbehaves at high angles could tumble on entry. Comparing three shapes on the same terms let designers pick the soundest line. The study belongs to the first wave of lifting entry research.
nasa-tm-19710022735-aerodynamic-characte:
William J. Monta of the Langley Research Center wrote this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2340, on an unusual missile shape. The model had a blunt, flat-faced nose and a body with a triangular cross section. Three fixed fins, a triform tail, provided its stability and control surfaces.

Wind tunnel tests in the Langley Unitary Plan tunnel covered speeds from Mach 1.60 to Mach 2.16 and many roll orientations. Monta varied nose corner radius, fin span, and fin asymmetry meant to produce rolling moment. Results show the model tended to pitch up in the flat-top orientation and pitch down in the flat-bottom one. A smaller nose corner radius mainly raised axial force, while a larger fin span moved the aerodynamic center rearward.
the-best-letters-of-charles-lamb:
Edward Gilpin Johnson edited a selection of Charles Lamb's letters in 1892, under a heading calling them laurel-crowned. Praise from A. C. Swinburne and W. C. Hazlitt stands at the front. Hazlitt claims no kindred collection matches the letters in range, period, or typical character.

Contents list letter after letter to Samuel Taylor Coleridge, eighteen in the opening run alone. Robert Southey follows as the next named recipient. The order shows Lamb's early writing life bound up with Coleridge. Readers get a famed essayist in private form, writing to poet friends rather than to the public of his Essays of Elia.
the-secret-tomb: Maurice Le Blanc's The Secret Tomb was copyrighted by The Macaulay Company in New York in 1923. Le Blanc is billed as creator of Arsene Lupin. George W. Gage supplied the frontispiece. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. The Château de Roborey opens the list. Dorothy's circus, extra lucid, and a cross-examination follow. We will help you is promised in chapter five. No story text appears here.
the-uphill-climb: B. M. Bower, author of Good Indian and Chip, of the Flying U, published The Uphill Climb with Grosset and Dunlap in 1913. Charles M. Russell illustrated the western. The pages present here hold the title page, a seventeen-chapter contents list, and an illustrations list, but no story text. Chapter one is titled Married! And I Don't Know Her Name. Later headings follow Ford through reaction, a plan gone wrong, and a fight with the Demon. Closing titles promise a climb and a search to free a wife.
the-wolves-and-the-lamb:
William Makepeace Thackeray's The Wolves and the Lamb is a play set at a villa in Richmond. The cast lists Horace Milliken, a wealthy widowed merchant. His mother-in-law, Lady Kicklebury, figures prominently. A governess, Miss Prior, cares for the Milliken children. Servants, a captain, and the Bonningtons round out the household.

Act one opens in two adjoining drawing rooms. The late Mrs. Milliken's portrait hangs over the mantelpiece. Bookcases, a piano, and newspapers furnish the rooms. Large windows look onto a lawn and pleasure ground. Thackeray sets a comfortable home where sharp social maneuvering can unfold.
universite-de-paris-faculte-de-theologie:
The Faculty of Theology of Paris addressed these humble petitions to the French king in 1730. Their grievance was a ruling by the Parlement, handed down on May 17 of that year, against a theology thesis defended on May 8 by a licentiate named Hassett. Bound with the petitions is the reply letter of the Comte de Maurepas, a secretary of state, written by order of the king.

The faculty open with thanks for recent royal favors, then say duty forces them to mix sorrow with gratitude. They argue that the ruling struck at their rights and honor, since the thesis had passed under their own authority. The French text keeps the old spelling and formal address of court papers of the time. Readers get a close look at a church faculty defending its turf against a royal court of law.
